response.title: how do i keep my insulin cold during a power outage
response.answer:
If your power goes out, the safest way to protect your insulin is to keep it between 36°F and 46°F (2°C–8°C) if it is unopened. But don't panic if your refrigerator stops working—many types of insulin can safely remain at room temperature for a limited period.

Here's what to do.

1. If the power just went out

Keep the refrigerator door closed. An unopened refrigerator generally stays cold for about 4 hours.

Don't immediately move your insulin. Keeping it in the closed refrigerator may be better than exposing it to warm air.

Check the temperature if you have a refrigerator thermometer.

Never freeze insulin. Insulin that has frozen should not be used, even after thawing.

2. If the outage lasts longer than 4 hours
Shop

Use an insulated cooler

Put your insulin in a sealed bag or protective container inside a cooler with cold packs. Wrap the cold packs in towels so the insulin never touches them directly.

Shop

Use a temperature-controlled insulin cooler

A battery-powered or rechargeable insulin refrigerator can be useful during extended outages. Make sure it maintains refrigerator temperatures without freezing the insulin.

Shop

Use an evaporative cooling pouch

Products such as FRIO cooling wallets work without electricity. They help protect insulin from heat but generally do not maintain refrigerator temperatures, so they're better for temporary temperature protection than long-term refrigerated storage.

3. How long can insulin stay unrefrigerated?

Many insulin products can be kept at temperatures up to 86°F (30°C) for approximately 28 days, but this varies by brand, formulation, and whether the container has been opened.

For example:

Insulin

	

Typical room-temperature limit




Humalog

	

28 days




NovoLog

	

28 days




Lantus

	

28 days




Tresiba

	

56 days

These are common limits for certain vial or pen presentations, not universal rules for every product. Always check the instructions for your exact insulin.

Important: Don't stop taking insulin simply because the power is out. If you're unsure whether your insulin is still usable, contact your pharmacist or diabetes care team promptly. Monitor blood glucose more frequently if you suspect heat exposure has affected its potency.

4. If you don't have ice or a cooler

Try to find a refrigerator with backup power at a friend’s home, pharmacy, hospital, or emergency shelter. Keep insulin away from direct sunlight, hot cars, and windows.

If your insulin has been exposed to excessive heat or has frozen, contact a pharmacist about replacement. Seek urgent medical help if your blood sugar stays very high, especially if you have ketones, vomiting, or difficulty breathing.

Two questions so I can give you more precise advice:

What insulin do you use? (Lantus, Humalog, NovoLog, Tresiba, or another brand?)

How long do you expect the power to be out? A few hours, one day, or several days?

The best storage approach depends on both.
